title: Lead by Following: Transformative Leadership Strategies
author: Leadership With a Twist
summary: This Leadership With a Twist post distills an episode in which executive coaches Heather McGonigal and Barbara Schindler argue that leaders get more from their teams by leading from behind. The central claim is that leaders who speak first in meetings unintentionally train their teams to nod along, and that the corrective is not more confidence but listening first. The piece defines active listening as drawing ideas forward with open questions rather than staying quiet, and recommends that leaders share a half-formed idea to give others permission to bring their own unfinished thinking. It then turns to leadership reputation, arguing that it is built in the hardest weeks when teams watch how a leader handles pressure, and that naming one's own default stress response is the first step toward changing it. The post ends with a practical challenge to practice listening first in a single recurring meeting for two to three weeks, alongside a short action list and reflection questions.
points: Speaking first in a meeting, the default move for someone with authority, is identified as the reason teams defer instead of pushing back.
Active listening is framed as asking questions like what are you seeing that I am not, so people offer unfinished thoughts rather than polished conclusions.
Sharing a half-baked idea yourself is recommended as the quickest way to open up a silent room.
Leadership reputation is said to be defined in high-pressure weeks, which makes knowing your stress default (shutting down or getting sharp) essential.
The coaches advise practicing one habit in one recurring meeting for two to three weeks rather than changing everything at once.
quotes: And then you wonder why your team just nods along instead of pushing back or adding their own thinking.
When you have the authority, the instinct is to use it first. Speak, direct, decide, move on. But the leaders who get the most out of their teams do the opposite.
It’s asking, “tell me more,” and “what are you seeing that I’m not,” so your team knows you actually want their unfinished thoughts, not just their polished conclusions.
And if the room goes quiet when you try this, the move is to share something half-baked yourself.
It’s not built in the good weeks. It’s built in the hard ones, the ones where deadlines are stacking up and you’re under pressure and your team is watching how you handle it.
Knowing your own default under stress, whether you shut down or get sharp, is the first move toward actually choosing something different.
